title: A double portion (2 Kings 2:1–15)
hook: Elijah rises in a whirlwind; Elisha picks up his mantle
carry: an old cloak lying on the ground

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Naboth's vineyard, Elijah met the king with one question: hast thou killed, and taken? Did you say a true word for someone wronged? Today is Elijah's last day on earth, and someone refuses to leave his side. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Everyone seems to know what's about to happen. Elijah and his student Elisha are walking from Gilgal, and Elijah says: stay here, the Lord has sent me on to Beth-el. Elisha answers with an oath: as the Lord lives, I will not leave thee. At Beth-el, a group of prophets comes out and asks Elisha, do you know the Lord will take your master today? Yes, I know, he says. Hold your peace. Then Jericho: the same request, the same oath, another band of prophets, the same answer. Then the Jordan. Elisha simply will not be sent away.
screen: `STAY HERE.` → `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` → `HOLD YOUR PEACE.`

segments.voice: At the Jordan, Elijah takes off his mantle, his rough prophet's cloak, rolls it up, and strikes the water. The river divides, and the two of them cross on dry ground. On the other side Elijah turns to his student. Ask what I shall do for thee, before I am taken. And Elisha asks: "let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me." In Israel's inheritance law, the firstborn son received a double share. Some readers hear Elisha asking to be the heir, the one who carries on the household. Some Jewish commentators also read it more literally, as twice his teacher's wonders. Elijah answers honestly: thou hast asked a hard thing. If you see me when I'm taken, it will be so. If not, it won't. And as they walk and talk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha sees it, and cries out: my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof. Then he tears his own clothes in two. Grief first. And then he bends down and picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah. He walks back to the Jordan. He strikes the water with that same cloak and asks, where is the Lord, the God of Elijah? The water divides again. The prophets watching from Jericho say: the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. Notice that the inheritance doesn't arrive as a feeling. It arrives as an old cloak lying on the ground, and a river that still has to be crossed. In Jewish tradition Elijah never quite leaves the story: tradition says he will return to announce redemption, and a cup is poured for him at the Passover seder.
screen: `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` · `THE FIRSTBORN'S SHARE.` · then, large: `A DOUBLE PORTION OF THY SPIRIT.` · then: `THE MANTLE ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry on someone's good work. Let your hands rest open in your lap. Think of someone who taught you, cared for you, or started something good and then moved on, or passed on: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a neighbor. What did they do that you admired? Name one piece of it. A way of welcoming people, a recipe, a habit of calling on the lonely, a craft. That's the mantle on the ground. Then choose how to pick it up: one small way you could carry that work forward this week. If you pray, you can remember them by name. The bell holds the time.
Pi shnayim. The Hebrew for a double portion, the share Elisha asked for as his teacher was taken. Today's word.
Your line: an old cloak lying on the ground. Today, pick up one piece of good work someone left you, and do it once, in their honor. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Jews remember Elijah at the Passover seder with a cup poured for him, and the song Eliyahu HaNavi, asking for his return, is sung at the end of Shabbat.

fork.setup: you're Elisha. your teacher asks what he can do for you before he's taken. what do you ask for?
options: that he stay a little longer.
a double portion of his spirit.
fork.reveal: Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit. Elijah says it's a hard thing: if you see me taken, it will be so.

original.note: Hebrew: pi shnayim, a double portion, in 2 Kings 2:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: Elisha simply wanted twice his teacher's power.
what it means: Elisha asks to carry on his teacher's work, and then has to pick up the cloak himself.
what a scholar hears: pi shnayim is the firstborn's share in Deuteronomy 21:17; some Jewish commentators also read it as twice Elijah's wonders.

notes: Auditor (2026-10-01): SERIOUS: the myth called "Elisha wanted twice as much" a misconception, but rabbinic tradition reads pi shnayim literally (Elisha's wonders counted as double Elijah's); replaced myth, teach and trapdoor now give both readings. Fixed garbled trapdoor line. Keeper: cite the source for the doubled-wonders tradition.

Editor: the Jericho prophets are a different band, not 'the same prophets'; cut the narrator's verdict on what a double portion is not and the literal 'mouth of two' etymology; the heir reading is now framed as 'some readers' in myth and trapdoor; practice no longer says 'picture'.
Verify JPS 1917 wording at 2 Kings 2:9 ('let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me'); KJV reads the same.
The firstborn reading rests on pi shnayim in Deuteronomy 21:17; Keeper should confirm the phrase is the same there.
Dialogue at 2:2–6, 2:10, 2:12, 2:14–15 is paraphrased close to KJV without quotation marks.

Elijah's return to announce redemption is attributed to 'tradition says' (Malachi 3:23 in Jewish numbering); seder cup and Eliyahu HaNavi in howItsDone; 'many sing' is a soft claim, Keeper may adjust.
'Elijah's last day on earth' in the review follows the text's framing (2:1, 2:11).
